title: Tired or dizzy? Try salt
claim: Fatigue, headache or light-headedness while fasting is often low salt and water, not low energy.
why: Falling insulin makes the kidneys flush sodium and water. A pinch of salt usually helps within minutes.
do: Sit down, take a pinch of salt in water, and rise slowly. If it persists, end the fast.
label: emerging

title: Loose stools early on
claim: Some people get loose stools in early fasts as the body sheds retained water. It usually settles within days.
why: Falling insulin releases water the body was holding; some leaves through the bowel instead of the kidneys.
do: Psyllium husk in water can help. Persistent diarrhea or signs of dehydration mean stop and seek advice.
label: clinical experience

title: Heartburn while fasting
claim: Heartburn can worsen on an empty stomach, though for some it improves. Weight loss usually relieves reflux over time.
why: The stomach still makes acid with nothing to absorb it, and belly fat presses upward.
do: Finish eating 3 hours before bed, walk after dinner, raise the head of the bed. Ask about antacids if needed.
label: emerging

title: Magnesium: pick the right form
claim: Muscle cramps while fasting can mean low magnesium. If you supplement, choose citrate or glycinate over oxide.
why: Blood tests miss low tissue magnesium. Oxide is poorly absorbed and mostly acts as a laxative.
label: emerging

title: First-day headache?
claim: A headache in your first fasts is usually low salt, and it fades within a couple of weeks of regular fasting.
why: Going from salty meals to almost no salt changes fluid balance; the body adapts within a few fasts.
do: Add a pinch of salt to your water.
label: clinical experience

title: Constipation is normal
claim: Fewer bowel movements while fasting are normal and usually painless. With little food going in, little needs to come out.
why: Discomfort comes from a full colon, which a fasting colon isn't.
do: Eat more vegetables and fiber on eating days; psyllium helps. Ask your doctor if it persists.
label: emerging

title: Wired at night?
claim: Trouble sleeping or waking early on fasting days is common. Fasting raises energizing noradrenaline.
why: The same hormone that keeps you alert by day can delay sleep. It usually eases with practice.
do: Don't force sleep: wind down without screens, try a warm bath, go to bed when tired. If it persists, shorten or move fasts.
label: emerging

title: Feeling cold
claim: Feeling cold early in fasting is common and usually fades as your body gets better at burning fat. Layer up, drink hot, move.
why: New fasters can lag in switching to fat; movement uses circulating fuel and makes heat.
do: Cold all the time even when eating? Ask your doctor to check your thyroid.
label: clinical experience

title: Who shouldn't fast
claim: Don't fast for health if you're under 18, pregnant, breastfeeding, underweight (BMI under about 20), or have ever had an eating disorder.
why: Growth, pregnancy and milk need a steady nutrient supply, low body weight leaves no reserve, and deliberate restriction can reignite disordered eating.
do: If any of these apply, skip fasting and talk to your doctor about what's right for you.
label: established

title: Over 65? Protect your muscle
claim: After 65, weight loss takes muscle and bone with it unless you protect them. Choose shorter fasts and eat protein at every meal.
why: Older muscle responds less to protein. In dieting older adults, adding resistance plus aerobic exercise preserved lean mass and bone.
do: Strength-train 2–3 times a week, and stand up slowly to avoid dizziness.
label: established

title: Hungry is fine. Sick is not.
claim: Hunger is expected. Persistent nausea, vomiting, dizziness, exhaustion, or feeling truly unwell mean stop.
why: Hunger comes in waves and passes. These signs fall outside normal adaptation and can mean dehydration, electrolyte trouble or a medication problem.
do: End the fast, eat something gentle, and contact your doctor if it doesn't settle. Stopping isn't failing.
label: established

title: Beyond 3 days, involve a doctor
claim: Don't fast longer than about three days on your own. Longer fasts need medical supervision, blood tests and a refeeding plan.
why: Very long fasts in 1960s hospital programs caused rare deaths and heart damage. Normal blood tests can hide depleted stores; magnesium ran low in the 382-day fast.
do: For supervised long fasts: salt in your water, a multivitamin, and don't attempt them more than monthly.
label: emerging

title: Refeeding after long fasts
claim: After fasts of five days or more, restart eating with small meals. Refeeding syndrome is rare but dangerous.
why: Food raises insulin, which pulls phosphorus, potassium, magnesium and thiamine into cells; blood levels can crash. Highest risk: BMI under 18.5, recent big weight loss, alcohol misuse, diuretics or antacids.
do: Seek care for weakness, palpitations, confusion or breathlessness. Mild ankle swelling in the first days usually passes.
label: established

title: No alcohol while fasting
claim: Don't drink alcohol during a fast. It stops the liver making glucose, so blood sugar can fall, and it hits much harder.
why: The liver prioritizes clearing alcohol over gluconeogenesis; an empty stomach raises blood alcohol fast. On any day it disrupts sleep and adds empty energy.
do: If you drink, keep it with a meal on an eating day, with water alongside.
label: established

title: If your period stops
claim: Your cycle may shift in the first months of fasting. If periods stop for three months or more, stop fasting and see your doctor.
why: Occasional delays follow any change in weight, diet or stress. Missing periods mean energy availability is too low for reproductive health.
label: established

title: Condition or daily medicine?
claim: Diagnosed condition or daily medication? Turn on Health conditions in Settings to see only the guidance that applies to you.
why: Medicines for blood sugar, blood pressure, mood, thyroid or inflammation change how fasting affects you. Specific guidance is safer than generic warnings.
do: Talk to your doctor before your first fast longer than a day.
label: clinical experience

title: Use fasting aids sparingly
claim: A spoon of olive oil or chia soaked in water can rescue a fast. Use one only when it decides whether you finish.
why: Tiny amounts of fat or fiber barely raise insulin and blunt cravings; taken out of habit, they replace energy your fat stores would otherwise supply.
do: Ask: "Will this help me fast another 12 hours?"
label: clinical experience

title: Sweeteners make it harder
claim: Diet drinks, sweeteners and "naturally flavored" drinks tend to make fasting harder; swapping diet drinks for water improved weight loss in a trial.
why: Sweet taste may prime appetite and insulin without delivering energy, so cravings stay alive, especially near the end of a fast.
do: Fast with plain drinks. If you need sweetness, use a little and drop it if hunger worsens.
counter: Whether sweeteners raise insulin in humans is inconsistent across studies.
label: emerging

title: Yes while fasting
claim: Water (still or sparkling), any plain or herbal tea, lemon, cinnamon, salt, and plain vitamins or electrolytes.
why: These carry almost no energy, so insulin stays low, while they ease hunger, hydrate, and keep your daily rituals.
label: clinical experience

title: No while fasting
claim: Sugar, honey, juice, sweetened or flavored drinks, and sweeteners break or undermine a fast.
why: Sugars raise insulin outright. Juice concentrates sugar without fiber. Sweeteners and flavor additives tend to stoke appetite.
label: clinical experience

title: Drink on a schedule
claim: Aim for about 2 liters of fluid on fasting days. Start the morning with a glass of water.
why: Much of your usual water comes with food; as insulin falls you also shed retained water and salt. It's easy to forget to drink.
do: A reminder every couple of hours helps early on: water with a pinch of salt, or tea.
label: clinical experience

title: Teas that help
claim: Green tea, cinnamon or ginger teas and bitter herbal teas may take the edge off hunger; peppermint eases bloating.
why: Warm, flavorful, zero-energy drinks fill the stomach and keep the ritual. Green-tea catechins and cinnamon have mild appetite effects in small studies.
label: early research

title: Break it gently
claim: After fasts over 24 hours, start with a small "pre-meal": cooked vegetables or avocado. Main meal 30 minutes later.
why: Digestion slows during a fast. A small, easy first portion wakes it gently and lets the urge to feast pass.
do: Under 24 hours, no special care is needed. For longer fasts, prepare the small dish in advance.
label: clinical experience

title: Go easy on these first
claim: Right after a fast, nuts, seeds, nut butters, raw or fibrous vegetables, eggs, dairy and wine are the likeliest to upset your stomach.
why: They demand more stomach acid and enzymes, which take time to return after a fast. Tolerance varies by person.
label: clinical experience

title: Eat normally, not a feast
claim: The most common fasting mistake is eating too much afterward. Eat a normal-sized meal, as if the fast hadn't happened.
why: The fast works because stored fat covers the skipped meals. After a 36-hour fast people eat only ~20% more, but cramming a day's food into one meal cancels the gain.
do: Serve a normal portion, eat slowly, drink water, and wait before seconds. No extra calorie-cutting on top.
label: emerging

title: Carbs last
claim: Eat protein and vegetables first and carbs last. The same meal raised blood sugar about 40% less that way.
why: Protein, fat and fiber eaten first slow stomach emptying and prime gut hormones, so starch arrives later and gentler.
do: Leave bread, rice or potato for the end of the meal. Ask restaurants to bring bread with the main course.
label: emerging

title: No naked carbs
claim: Pair starch with acid, protein or fat: vinegar, lemon, pickles, or cooked-then-cooled rice and potatoes blunt the blood-sugar spike.
why: Acid slows starch digestion and stomach emptying; cooling cooked starch creates resistant starch; less processed versions (steel-cut vs instant oats) absorb slower.
label: emerging

title: Fullness hormones from food
claim: Protein, natural fat and fiber trigger your gut's own fullness hormones, the same pathway weight-loss drugs amplify.
why: These nutrients slow stomach emptying and release GLP-1; fiber feeds gut bacteria whose fatty acids boost it further.
do: Build meals around protein, natural fats and fibrous vegetables to stay full longer.
counter: Natural GLP-1 rises are far smaller than drug effects.
label: emerging

title: Real food beats processed
claim: Ultra-processed food made people eat about 500 kcal more per day than whole food with the same nutrients.
why: Processing strips fiber and structure, speeds eating and absorption, and weakens fullness signals; sugar and refined flour do this most.
do: Fill eating windows with recognizable whole foods; cut sugar and white flour first.
label: established

title: Breakfast food is often dessert
claim: Cereals, muffins, pastries, sweetened yogurt and breakfast bars are often dessert in disguise, and leave you ravenous by mid-morning.
why: Refined carbs spike glucose and insulin, which then overshoot; an instant-oatmeal breakfast led children to eat more later than an omelet did.
do: If you eat breakfast, make it eggs, plain yogurt or whole oats, or simply delay your first meal.
label: emerging

title: Sugar and liver fat
claim: Sugar's fructose is turned into fat in the liver. Cutting added sugar shrank liver fat by about a third in eight weeks.
why: Fructose is processed almost only by the liver. Fatty liver affects a quarter or more of adults, usually silently; 5:2 fasting and low-carb both halved it in a trial.
label: established

title: Eat earlier when you can
claim: The same meal raises blood sugar and insulin more in the evening. A lighter, earlier dinner suits your body clock.
why: Insulin sensitivity is lowest at night; eating at biological night (shift work, late meals) worsens glucose and lowers fullness hormones.
do: Make dinner lighter and earlier; on night shifts, eat the main meal before the shift.
counter: In a tightly controlled trial, big breakfast vs big dinner didn't change weight, only hunger.
label: established
src: Scheer 2009 Proc Natl Acad Sci USA

title: Protein and lifting protect muscle
claim: Strength training and enough protein when you eat are what protect muscle during fasting; fasting alone doesn't.
why: Muscle responds to load. Fasting combined with resistance training preserves lean mass far better than fasting alone.
do: Lift or do bodyweight training 2–3 times a week; aim for ~1.2–1.6 g protein per kg body weight on eating days.
label: established

title: After a meal: storing
claim: After eating, blood sugar peaks within about an hour and insulin rises. While insulin is high, fat burning is paused.
why: Insulin moves glucose into cells, banks the surplus as glycogen and fat, and blocks fat release until levels fall.
label: established

title: A short walk after eating
claim: A 10–15 minute easy walk after a meal noticeably lowers the blood-sugar and insulin spike from it.
why: Working muscles take up glucose with little need for insulin; light walking beat standing in a meta-analysis of crossover trials.
do: Walk after your biggest meal, especially one with bread, rice, pasta or dessert.
label: emerging

title: The 3-hour slump
claim: Ravenous a few hours after a sugary or starchy meal? That's often a blood-sugar rebound, not a real lack of fuel.
why: A fast glucose spike calls up a big insulin surge that can overshoot, dipping glucose below baseline about three hours later.
do: Ride it out with water or tea. Next time, eat protein and vegetables first and carbs last.
label: emerging

title: Insulin settles, fat unlocks
claim: A few hours after a meal (roughly 3–5, longer with insulin resistance), insulin returns to baseline and fat cells start releasing fat.
why: Low insulin lifts the brake on fat release while the liver draws on glycogen. A snack raises insulin again and pushes this switch back.
do: Let this window happen: no snacks between meals.
label: emerging

title: The liver takes over
claim: Overnight and into the morning, your liver keeps blood sugar steady, first from stored glycogen, then increasingly by making new glucose.
why: The liver holds about 100 g of glycogen. By around 22 hours, newly made glucose (from glycerol, lactate and amino acids) supplies most of the output.
label: established

title: Fridge and freezer
claim: Glycogen is the fridge: small and quick. Body fat is the basement freezer: vast. Low insulin opens the freezer door.
why: The body draws on glycogen first. High insulin keeps fat locked away; as insulin falls and glycogen runs low, stored fat becomes the main fuel.
do: Every hour after the fridge empties is an hour drawn from the freezer. That's what fasting buys.
counter: Insulin's block on fat release is textbook. That insulin, rather than overall energy balance, causes obesity is contested.
label: emerging

title: The switch is personal
claim: The shift to burning mostly fat and ketones typically happens 12–36 hours after your last meal, earlier for some, later for others.
why: Timing depends on how full your glycogen was. A carb-heavy dinner and sitting still push it later; lower-carb meals and movement bring it sooner.
do: A walk during the fast, and a lower-carb last meal, both speed the switch.
label: emerging

title: Ketones feed the brain
claim: Your brain isn't glucose-only. As fasting continues it runs increasingly on ketones, and studies find no loss of attention or memory.
why: Liver-made ketones cross into the brain and replace much of its glucose need. That spares muscle protein and keeps you alert.
do: Work and drive normally. If you feel foggy, check salt and water first.
counter: The brain's ketone share reaches ~60–70% only after weeks; in the first days it's lower.
label: established

title: Autophagy, honestly
claim: Fasting boosts autophagy, your cells' recycling of worn-out parts. But no one knows exactly when it starts or peaks in humans.
why: Eating, especially protein and carbs, switches autophagy off through mTOR. Human markers rise after 24–36-hour fasts, but popular hour thresholds come from animal studies.
do: Long gaps without snacks give cells time with the brake released. Treat any hour count as an estimate.
label: early research

title: Day two is the hardest
claim: In longer fasts hunger usually peaks around day two, then fades. Many people feel unusually clear and well afterward.
why: Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, peaks on day two and then falls as ketones rise; hospital fasting reports note little hunger after that.
do: If day two is rough, expect it to ease. Don't judge the whole fast by its hardest day.
label: emerging

title: What the scale is saying
claim: Real fat loss while fasting is about 0.25 kg (½ lb) a day. The rest of the drop is water that returns when you eat.
why: A day's energy (~2,000 kcal) burns about a quarter-kilo of fat. Glycogen is stored with roughly three times its weight in water, which is released, then refilled.
do: Judge a fast by the weight still off a week later.
label: established

title: Growth hormone rises
claim: Fasting is a strong natural booster of growth hormone: about fivefold over a two-day fast.
why: Meals and insulin suppress GH. Without food its pulses grow, helping release fat and restraining muscle-protein breakdown.
counter: A fuel-sparing signal, not anti-aging or muscle-building. IGF-1 falls at the same time; studies are small, in lean men.
label: emerging

title: No starvation mode in short fasts
claim: Short fasts don't put you in "starvation mode". Resting energy use rose about 12% by day four.
why: Noradrenaline rises to release stored fuel and keep you alert enough to find food: the opposite of shutting down.
do: Expect energy, not sluggishness. Fatigue usually signals low salt.
counter: Small study of lean adults. Much longer fasts do eventually lower energy use.
label: emerging

title: Saving sugar for the brain
claim: Two to three days in, muscles temporarily resist insulin to save glucose for the brain. It's normal and reverses after eating.
why: Fat released from stores floods muscle and blocks its glucose uptake. Higher readings late in a long fast, or just after it, are expected.
do: Judge insulin health between fasts: repeated fasting with fat loss improves it over weeks.
label: emerging

title: Muscle is spared, not untouched
claim: Protein breakdown is highest in the first days of a fast, then falls sharply as ketones take over. It slows; it never stops.
why: Early glucose comes partly from amino acids. As ketones rise, nitrogen loss drops; in a 10-day trial, strength held while lean tissue declined slightly.
do: Protect muscle with strength training and enough protein on eating days.
label: established

title: Renewal: what's known
claim: Multi-day fasts in mice clear old immune cells and trigger regeneration on refeeding. In people this remains unproven.
why: Prolonged fasting lowers IGF-1 and growth signaling, pushing stem cells toward self-renewal; ordinary daily fasting barely moves IGF-1.
label: early research

title: Keep moving
claim: Do your usual activities while fasting: walk, work, lift. Movement protects muscle and bone during longer fasts.
why: Stored fat supplies the energy. Disuse, not fasting itself, drove most muscle and bone loss in famous long fasts done lying still.
do: Walk daily and keep light strength work going; scale back if you feel faint.
label: emerging

title: What fasting actually does
claim: Regular fasting lowers weight, insulin, blood sugar, blood pressure and inflammation, and it's simple, free and works with any diet.
why: It restricts all foods some of the time rather than some foods all the time. In trials most benefits track the weight lost, about matching daily dieting at equal loss.
do: Its real edge is adherence: pick the version you can keep.
label: established
src: de Cabo & Mattson 2019 N Engl J Med

title: Prediabetes is common and silent
claim: More than half of US adults have diabetes or prediabetes, and most with prediabetes don't know it.
why: Prediabetes rarely causes symptoms, so it goes unnoticed for years while damage starts.
do: Ask for an HbA1c or fasting glucose test, especially if you carry weight around the waist.
label: established

title: Fuel for a month
claim: Even a lean adult carries enough body fat to cover more than a month of energy needs.
why: At 70 kg and 15% body fat that's about 10 kg of fat, roughly 80,000 kcal, versus about 2,000 kcal of glycogen.
label: established

title: Diabetes medication? Plan first
claim: Fasting on insulin or diabetes pills without a plan can cause dangerous lows. Your doctor will usually lower doses on fasting days.
why: Most diabetes drugs are dosed for days you eat. Remove the food and the same dose overshoots; repeated lows mean the dose is too high, not that fasting failed.
do: Agree on doses and target ranges with your doctor, check sugar 2–4 times a day, and never adjust insulin on your own.
label: established

title: Know the signs of a low
claim: Shaking, sweating, sudden hunger, nervousness, confusion or faintness can mean low blood sugar, especially if you take diabetes medication.
why: Without medication, the liver keeps glucose steady (often 60–75 mg/dL in long fasts, without symptoms). With medication it can crash quickly, and severe lows are dangerous.
do: Take sugar right away (juice, glucose tablets), even though it ends the fast, then call your doctor.
label: established

title: Ketosis is not ketoacidosis
claim: Fasting ketosis is normal. Ketoacidosis is different and dangerous, and it's a risk with type 1 diabetes or SGLT2 drugs (names ending in "-gliflozin").
why: In ketosis, insulin is low but present and ketones are burned as fuel. In ketoacidosis, too little insulin lets ketones pile up, sometimes even with normal blood sugar.
do: Type 1 diabetes or a "-gliflozin" drug: don't fast without your doctor's explicit plan.
label: established

title: When fasting stops lowering sugar
claim: If fasting no longer brings your blood sugar down, ask your doctor about LADA, a slow autoimmune diabetes often mistaken for type 2.
why: In LADA insulin is low rather than high, so fasting helps far less and ketoacidosis becomes a risk. C-peptide and antibody tests tell them apart.
label: emerging

title: Blood-pressure pills and fasting
claim: Fasting lowers blood pressure. On blood-pressure pills or diuretics it can drop too low, causing light-headedness when you stand.
why: Falling insulin makes the kidneys shed salt and water, which adds to the medication's effect.
do: Check your pressure at home while fasting, rise slowly, and let your doctor adjust doses. Never stop heart medication on your own.
label: established

title: Medicines that need food
claim: Aspirin, metformin, iron and magnesium pills can upset an empty stomach. Ask whether to take them in your eating window.
why: Aspirin irritates the stomach lining; metformin causes nausea or diarrhea; iron causes pain and constipation; magnesium causes loose stools. Food buffers them.
do: Never just skip a prescribed medicine. Your pharmacist can help you time doses.
label: established

title: Steroids: never skip doses
claim: If you take steroid replacement for adrenal insufficiency, or long-term prednisone, don't fast without your endocrinologist, and never skip a dose.
why: Without enough cortisol the body can't hold up blood sugar and blood pressure during a fast; adrenal crisis is a real risk.
label: established

title: Lithium or warfarin? Check first
claim: On lithium, dehydration or less salt can push levels toward toxicity. On warfarin, changing how you eat can shift your INR.
why: Kidneys handle lithium like sodium and hold it when salt and water fall. Warfarin's effect depends on steady vitamin K intake and liver metabolism.
do: Agree a plan with your prescriber, stay well hydrated, and get levels checked more often when you start.
label: emerging

title: Thyroid medication and fasting
claim: On thyroid medication, recheck your levels when you start fasting or lose weight. The dose you need may change.
why: Weight loss and calmer inflammation can lower the requirement; symptoms are a poor guide. Fast longer only once levels are stable, not while a dose is being adjusted.
do: Racing heart, anxiety, heat intolerance or poor sleep while fasting: get your thyroid checked.
label: emerging

title: On Ozempic-type drugs
claim: On semaglutide or tirzepatide, prioritize protein, strength training and fluids over longer fasts, and plan any fasting with your prescriber.
why: These drugs already cut appetite steeply, so muscle loss and dehydration from nausea become the risks. Combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, lows become likelier.
do: Use the time to build lasting habits: within a year of stopping, two-thirds of the lost weight typically returns.
label: emerging
src: Ramadan GLP-1RA systematic review 2025 World J Methodol (PMID 40900863)
Wilding 2022 Diabetes Obes Metab (STEP 1 extension, PMID 35441470)

title: Gout or kidney stones
claim: Fasting raises uric acid. If you've had gout or kidney stones, talk to your doctor before longer fasts, and drink plenty.
why: Ketones compete with uric acid for removal by the kidneys, and less fluid concentrates urine. About 6% on long-term ketogenic diets developed stones.
do: Keep urine pale; ask whether to continue uric-acid medication during fasts.
label: emerging

title: Kidney, heart or cancer: specialist first
claim: With kidney disease, heart disease or cancer, fast only with your specialist's agreement, even though early studies look promising.
why: Small trials show benefits (better heart recovery after infarction, less kidney protein in diabetes), but electrolytes, medications and weight loss carry bigger risks in these conditions.
do: With kidney disease, take magnesium or potassium supplements only with your doctor's approval.
label: emerging

title: Gallstones and fast weight loss
claim: Rapid weight loss raises gallstone risk. Include some natural fat at meals, and check with your doctor if you've had gallbladder attacks.
why: Bile that sits unused in the gallbladder can crystallize into stones. Very low-fat eating and rapid loss both increase stasis.
label: emerging

title: Blood-sugar herbs add up
claim: Bitter melon, cinnamon and some teas may lower blood sugar. On diabetes medication, that adds to the risk of lows.
why: Their modest glucose-lowering effect stacks on top of the drug's, and a fast removes the food that buffers it.
label: early research

title: PCOS and insulin
claim: PCOS, the most common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age, is driven by insulin resistance, even in lean women.
why: High insulin pushes the ovaries to overproduce androgens and disrupts ovulation; lowering insulin often restores regular cycles.
do: Irregular periods, acne or excess hair with belly weight? Ask your doctor about PCOS.
label: established
src: Brito Pateguana & Fung 2020 The PCOS Plan

title: Type 2 is too much insulin
claim: In type 2 diabetes insulin is usually high, not low, and it can often be put into remission through diet.
why: Fat in the liver and pancreas drives resistance and impairs insulin release; losing it can restore control, especially early in the disease.
do: Track remission with your doctor through HbA1c. Never stop medication on your own.
label: established

title: High morning sugar while fasting
claim: Higher blood sugar in the morning or during a long fast isn't failure. It's your liver releasing stored sugar.
why: Before waking and during fasting, hormones push stored glucose out (the dawn phenomenon). With insulin resistance, blood tests show it.
do: Watch the trend over weeks, not one reading.
label: emerging

title: Religious fasts with a condition
claim: With diabetes, kidney disease or on diuretics, religious dry fasts need a plan from your doctor, and most traditions allow exemptions or water.
why: Food and water restriction together raise the risk of dehydration, low blood sugar and low blood pressure; Ramadan guidelines stratify risk and adjust medication timing.
label: established

title: A rhythm, not a punishment
claim: Fasting isn't penance for overeating. Use it as a planned rhythm, not to "make up" for a meal.
why: Restricting to compensate is a recognized warning pattern for disordered eating, and it turns food into guilt.
label: clinical experience

title: Hunger comes in waves
claim: Hunger builds, peaks and fades, often within 30–45 minutes, even if you eat nothing. It doesn't keep climbing.
why: Ghrelin spikes around your usual mealtimes and then drops on its own, whether or not food arrives.
do: Drink something warm, start a task, step outside. Plan a walk or call for your usual mealtime.
label: emerging

title: Mornings are easiest
claim: Most people are least hungry around 8 a.m. and hungriest around 8 p.m., regardless of when they last ate.
why: Appetite follows the body clock, and pre-dawn hormones release stored fuel before you wake.
do: Extending the overnight fast by delaying breakfast is often the easiest first step.
label: emerging

title: Much hunger is learned
claim: Clocks, places, screens and smells can trigger hunger like Pavlov's bell. Notice the cue and name it: cue, not need.
why: Repeatedly pairing food with times and situations conditions the brain to release saliva, insulin and hunger on cue.
do: Eat only at a table; don't cook, shop or work in the kitchen on fasting days.
label: established

title: An if-then plan
claim: Decide in advance what you'll do when hunger hits: "If I open the fridge, I walk for ten minutes."
why: Pre-planned responses to specific cues reliably beat willpower. Swapping a habit (tea instead of the evening snack) works better than dropping it.
do: Keep 3–5 quick actions ready: water, tea, a walk, a call, a small chore.
label: established

title: Make hunger your friend
claim: Hunger during a fast means you're on track, not in danger. With regular fasting, appetite tends to fall over time.
why: Hunger is mostly a passing hormonal and habit signal; treating it as an expected companion lowers anxiety, and the body adapts with practice.
label: clinical experience

title: Give it a month
claim: The first few fasts are usually the hardest. Judge fasting by your fifth attempt, not your first.
why: Hunger habits, conditioned responses and fuel switching all adapt with repetition; your body learns to move into fat-burning faster.
do: The night before, eat a simple home-cooked meal low in sugar and starch; it makes the next day easier.
label: clinical experience

title: Ending early still counts
claim: A fast that ends early still counts. Stopping at 22 of 24 hours is 22 hours of benefit, not a failure.
why: Benefits build hour by hour. Treating partial fasts as wins builds the confidence that makes longer ones possible.
label: clinical experience

title: A nibble doesn't reset it
claim: A few nuts, a piece of cheese or a bite of salad doesn't reset your fast to zero. Just carry on.
why: A tiny intake bumps insulin briefly, then it falls again and fat-burning resumes. Missing a fast day doesn't undo weeks of routine either.
do: Note it if you like and continue. Back on schedule tomorrow.
label: clinical experience

title: Not during stress or travel
claim: Long fasts often fail during travel, stress or celebrations. Schedule them for quieter weeks.
why: Fasting is itself a stressor. On top of other stress it raises cortisol and blood sugar and turns from beneficial to draining.
do: In a high-stress period, shorten fasts rather than push harder.
label: clinical experience

title: Don't do it alone
claim: People who fast with a partner, friend or group do better, especially at keeping weight off.
why: Shared schedules remove food cues at home, and accountability keeps habits going after the early motivation fades.
do: Invite someone to fast with you, or tell a few supportive people. Not everyone.
label: emerging

title: Food between fasts matters
claim: You can't out-fast an unhealthy diet. If a longer fast leads to overeating, dial back down: not ready yet, not weak.
why: Poor eating between fasts gradually cancels their benefit and makes the next fast harder. Progress sticks when each level is steady before the next.
do: Notice why you eat (habit, comfort, company) without shame, and lengthen fasts only once meals are steady.
label: clinical experience

title: Sleep is part of it
claim: Short sleepers who slept about an hour more ate ~270 kcal less a day and lost weight without any diet advice.
why: Sleep loss raises hunger and food reward and lowers insulin sensitivity. Chronic stress adds cortisol and stress eating.
do: Under 6.5 hours of sleep? An earlier bedtime may be your easiest lever.
label: established
src: Al Khatib 2017 Eur J Clin Nutr

title: One slip isn't a lost day
claim: A slip is one meal, not a ruined day. All-or-nothing thinking turns small lapses into big ones; kindness to yourself prevents it.
why: After breaking a rule, restrained eaters often eat far more (the "what-the-hell" effect). Self-compassion after a lapse reduced later overeating; self-criticism increased it.
do: Resume at the next planned point, and talk to yourself as you would to a friend.
label: emerging
src: Adams & Leary 2007 J Soc Clin Psychol

title: Surf the urge
claim: A craving is a wave. Notice where you feel it, breathe, and watch it crest and fade without acting on it.
why: Observing an urge without judging it breaks the automatic craving-to-action chain; brief "urge surfing" training weakened that link in a controlled trial.
counter: Tested for smoking; food-specific evidence is smaller, though the mechanism is shared.
label: emerging

title: Picture two hours later
claim: Before an unplanned bite, picture how you'll feel in two hours and tomorrow. It measurably cools the craving.
why: Long-term framing recruits the brain's prefrontal control regions and dampens reward-region responses to the craved food.
label: emerging
src: Kober 2010 Proc Natl Acad Sci USA (PMID 20679212)

title: Cues are a real force
claim: Food sights, smells and ads reliably drive eating and weight gain, and the urge they create often exceeds the pleasure the food delivers.
why: Dopamine fuels "wanting"; enjoyment runs on separate circuits. Cues inflate wanting without adding liking, so avoiding them is strategy, not weakness.
label: established

title: We eat more together
claim: People eat substantially more with others than alone, most of all with friends and family.
why: Shared meals last longer and set portion norms; a meta-analysis found this social facilitation reliable.
do: Plan fasts around social meals rather than fighting them, and decide your portion before you sit down.
label: established

title: Next milestone, not the finish
claim: Aim for the next milestone on the dial, not the end of the fast. Motivation rises as a goal gets close.
why: The goal-gradient effect: effort increases with perceived nearness, so a chain of near targets carries you further than one distant finish line.
label: emerging

title: Bored, or hungry?
claim: Much "hunger" is boredom. People eat to escape the empty feeling of under-stimulation.
why: Eating offers quick stimulation and pulls attention away from an unpleasant state of low engagement.
do: Ask "hungry, or under-stimulated?" A task, a walk or a conversation often answers it.
label: emerging

title: Finishing builds confidence
claim: Every fast you complete makes the next one feel more doable. Personal success is the strongest source of self-confidence.
why: Self-efficacy grows mainly from mastery experiences, not persuasion, and it predicts whether a new habit lasts.
do: Start with fasts you can finish, then stretch. Count your completed fasts, not your misses.
label: emerging

title: Start by cutting snacks
claim: The easiest first fast: three meals, nothing in between. Most adults now eat 5–6 times a day, leaving almost no low-insulin time.
why: Each snack raises insulin again and works like an appetizer, stoking appetite. Removing snacks restores a daily fat-burning window at almost no hunger cost.
do: Then drop meals one at a time. The same path works for restarting after a break.
label: emerging
src: Popkin & Duffey 2010 Am J Clin Nutr

title: The best schedule is repeatable
claim: There's no single best fasting schedule. The right one is the one you can keep, and you can change it anytime.
why: Short daily fasts (16:8, one meal a day) are easiest to sustain; longer, less frequent fasts act faster on blood sugar and liver fat but are harder socially.
do: Build a routine around a daily window; add longer fasts in quiet weeks.
label: clinical experience

title: An eating window alone is modest
claim: In large trials, a 16:8 window alone gave little extra weight loss. Benefits come mostly from eating less and better within it.
why: When calories were matched, time-restricted eating did no better than ordinary calorie restriction. Fung's Fasting Method team treats 16:8 as maintenance and uses longer fasts for fat loss.
do: Use the window as structure, then fill it with whole, protein-rich food and no grazing.
counter: Early-day eating windows improved insulin sensitivity and blood pressure even without weight loss.
label: established

title: The 24-hour fast
claim: Dinner to dinner: you still eat one meal that day, so family dinners and food-needing medicines stay possible.
why: Skipping breakfast and lunch gives a full day of low insulin with little disruption. Two or three a week is a common rhythm.
label: clinical experience

title: The 36- and 42-hour fasts
claim: A 36-hour fast skips one whole day, dinner to breakfast two days later; skip that breakfast too and it's 42 hours.
why: It spans two nights of sleep. Fung's clinic uses these three times a week for type 2 diabetes, under supervision, then eases off.
label: clinical experience

title: 5:2 and alternate days
claim: 5:2 means two low days (~500–600 kcal) a week. Alternate-day fasting repeats that every other day; both work about as well as daily dieting.
why: A small allowance makes fast days easier. In trials, weight loss matched daily calorie cutting; insulin sometimes improved more, but dropout was higher.
label: established

title: Skip breakfast or dinner?
claim: Skipping breakfast is easiest; skipping dinner is most effective. Choose by what your day allows.
why: Breakfast is small, little-hungry and rarely social. Dinner is the biggest meal, eaten when insulin responses run highest, but it's the social one.
label: clinical experience

title: Fit fasting into your life
claim: Fit fasting into your life, not your life into fasting. Feast at celebrations, then fast in the days after.
why: Humans have always paired feasts with fasts. Much of the year's weight gain lands in the winter holidays; balance over weeks matters more than one meal.
do: Big dinner tonight? Skip breakfast and lunch. Fast harder on busy weekdays, lighter on family weekends.
label: emerging

title: Train near the end
claim: A good time to exercise is toward the end of a fast, then break it with a protein-rich meal.
why: Late in a fast noradrenaline is high and fat-burning is running. A 3.5-day fast didn't reduce strength or endurance in one study.
do: Example: fast from dinner, train at noon, eat lunch after. Scale back if you feel faint.
label: emerging

title: Bones need load
claim: Bones strengthen only under load. Walking, stairs and resistance training protect them far more than calcium pills.
why: Bone remodels in response to mechanical stress; astronauts lose bone despite eating well. Daily movement matters as much as gym sessions.
label: established

title: Treatment, then maintenance
claim: Intensive fasting can be a time-limited treatment. Once you reach your goal, maintenance is much lighter.
why: Clinics run therapeutic protocols for months, then step down to daily eating windows plus occasional longer fasts after holidays.
label: clinical experience

title: Breaking a plateau
claim: Plateaus are normal. Change the stimulus: a longer fast, a different schedule, or a stricter fast without sweeteners.
why: Any routine reaches balance as weight lost on fasting days matches weight regained. A new pattern restarts progress.
do: Try 24 → 36 → 48 hours, one meal a day, or an occasional longer fast. Check snacking and sleep too.
label: clinical experience

title: Measure more than weight
claim: When the scale stalls, measure your waist or take a monthly photo. Aim to keep your waist under half your height.
why: Water shifts hide fat loss for weeks. Waist size tracks the visceral fat most tied to diabetes and heart disease.
label: established

title: Your body defends its weight
claim: After weight loss, appetite rises about 100 kcal a day per kilo lost, and metabolism slows. Regain is biology, not weak willpower.
why: The body defends a set weight like a thermostat. Most calorie-cutting diets plateau and rebound; Biggest Loser contestants burned ~500 kcal/day less, six years on.
do: Expect stronger hunger as you lose; regular fasting, protein and whole food help hold the line.
label: established

title: Breakfast isn't essential
claim: Skipping breakfast doesn't make you eat more overall: in trials, breakfast eaters ate ~260 kcal more a day and weren't lighter.
why: The next meal grows only slightly, so total intake falls. The pre-dawn hormone surge has already fueled you.
label: established

title: Smart scales misread fasting
claim: Body-fat scales and scans often report "muscle loss" during fasting that is really water and glycogen, and it returns when you eat.
why: These devices estimate lean mass assuming steady body water; fasting sheds water, which they read as lost muscle.
do: Track strength and waist size instead during fasting periods.
label: emerging

title: That "91% heart risk" headline
claim: The 2024 "8-hour eating raises heart-death risk 91%" story came from an unreviewed conference abstract built on two days of diet recall.
why: Participants weren't intentionally fasting, and diet quality and baseline differences weren't reported, which the AHA's own reviewer flagged.
label: emerging

title: Keep dry fasts short
claim: Fasting without water is harder and riskier and adds no benefit. Keep dry fasts within a day, as in religious practice.
why: Without water the body dehydrates alongside fasting, straining circulation and kidneys and limiting how long a fast can safely run, with no added metabolic benefit.
do: Drink well in the hours before and after a dry fast.
label: emerging

title: An ancient calendar
claim: Nearly every tradition sets regular fast days: lunar and weekday fasts in Hinduism, Orthodox Lent, Ramadan, Buddhist monks eating nothing after noon.
why: Long before metabolism was understood, cultures paired feasting with fasting as cleansing and discipline. Crete, the Mediterranean-diet model, fasted on many days a year.
label: clinical experience

title: Trying to conceive
claim: Trying to conceive? Avoid extended fasts after ovulation, since you may already be pregnant. Focus on full, nourishing meals instead.
why: Pregnancy is a reason not to fast. In the second half of the cycle you can't know yet, so shorter eating windows are the safer choice.
label: clinical experience

title: Fasting with your cycle
claim: Appetite is lower in the first half of the cycle and higher after ovulation. Plan longer fasts for days 2–14.
why: Estrogen suppresses appetite; progesterone stimulates it, and insulin sensitivity dips before your period, which makes that week the hardest.
do: In the week or two before your period, prefer shorter fasts and skip sweeteners between meals.
label: emerging

title: Weigh by the cycle
claim: Women's weight loss runs in a monthly wave. Compare weight at the same point in each cycle, not week to week.
why: Water retention rises in the second half of the cycle and drops after menstruation, masking fat loss.
label: emerging

title: Perimenopause shifts the rules
claim: In the years before menopause, women gain about 0.5 kg a year and lose lean mass. It's hormonal, not a lack of discipline.
why: Falling estrogen raises appetite and moves fat toward the belly; poor sleep speeds it. After menopause heart risk climbs toward men's.
do: Prioritize strength training, protein and sleep; fasting helps, but expect slower progress.
label: established

title: Women benefit too
claim: Women lose weight with fasting at about the same rate as men; a 3-day fast left reproductive hormones normal in normal-weight women.
why: Cycle problems come from low body fat and energy deficiency, not fasting itself, in women with adequate reserves.
counter: Lean, very active women face higher risk of energy deficiency; long-term women-specific data are limited.
label: emerging
